Protecting Your Own Privacy When Searching Public Records

Looking up public records leaves traces, and your own information may be searchable too. Practical steps for safer searching and for limiting what others can find about you.

Key takeaways

  • ✓Use official .gov sources and avoid entering sensitive identifiers like a Social Security number.
  • ✓Search your own name to see what is public, then ask the custodian about redaction or correction.
  • ✓Sealing, expungement, and address confidentiality programs depend on your state.

In this guide

  1. Searching More Safely
  2. What Records Show About You
  3. Ways to Limit Exposure
  4. Searching Responsibly

Public records are open by design, but that openness cuts both ways. Searching them can leave a trail, and the records you create in daily life, such as buying property, starting a business, or appearing in court, can make your own details easy to find. This guide covers two questions: how to search more safely, and how to reduce what others can learn about you.

Searching More Safely

The safest searches use official sources. Government portals ending in .gov, and the websites of county clerks, recorders, and courts, publish records directly. Commercial "people search" sites repackage that same data, sometimes with errors, and often push paid reports or sell the details of what you searched. If a site asks for payment to show "free" public information, check whether the official source offers it at no charge first.

  • Assume portals keep logs. Government sites may record IP addresses and, where an account is required, tie searches to that account. PACER, the federal court system, requires registration and tracks usage for billing.
  • Use a private connection. Avoid public Wi-Fi when logging into any records account.
  • Share as little as needed. You almost never need to enter a Social Security number to search a record. Be wary of any site that asks for one.
  • Check the address bar. Look-alike sites copy the appearance of official portals. Type the address yourself or follow links from a state or county homepage.

What Records Show About You

Common places your information appears include county property records (owner name and mailing address), court dockets, business filings (officer names and registered agent addresses), professional license databases, and campaign donation records. Run your own name through the county recorder, the courts where you have lived, and the Secretary of State business search to see what is visible.

Ways to Limit Exposure

  • Use a registered agent address for a business instead of your home address, where state law allows it.
  • Ask about address confidentiality programs. Many states run programs for survivors of domestic violence, stalking, and similar situations that provide a substitute address for public records and voter registration. Eligibility rules vary.
  • Know the redaction rules. Under the federal court rules, filers must redact Social Security numbers to the last four digits, birth dates to the year, minors' names to initials, and financial account numbers to the last four digits. Many state courts have similar rules. If sensitive data appears unredacted, contact the court clerk and ask about its process for correcting it.
  • Ask about sealing or expungement. Some records can be sealed or expunged. The eligibility rules are state-specific, and a legal aid office or attorney can tell you what applies.
  • Opt out of data brokers. Many commercial sites that republish public records provide an opt-out form. This removes the listing from that site, but it does not change the underlying government record.

Searching Responsibly

Public does not mean unrestricted. Records pulled for tenant screening, employment, or credit decisions fall under the Fair Credit Reporting Act when they come from a consumer reporting agency, and misusing personal information to harass or stalk someone can break state and federal law. Use records for legitimate purposes, such as verifying a business, researching a property, or understanding a court case.

Quick Checklist

  • Start at the official .gov source.
  • Never enter a Social Security number to run a search.
  • Search your own name to see what is public.
  • Look into address confidentiality or sealing if you have a safety concern.
  • Record the source, date, and case or document number of anything you rely on.

If Your Information Is Wrong or Exposed

  1. Identify the source. Find which office or website published the record.
  2. Contact the custodian. For a court record, contact the clerk. For a property or business record, contact the recorder or Secretary of State. Ask about their process for corrections or redaction.
  3. Put the request in writing. Include the case or document number, what is wrong, and why.
  4. Ask about legal options. Sealing, expungement, and redaction orders are decided by the court and differ by state. Legal aid organizations may help at low or no cost.
  5. Follow up with brokers. If third-party sites copied the record, use their opt-out forms.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can someone see that I looked up a record? Usually not another member of the public, but the website operator may log activity, and some systems that require an account link searches to that account.

Are free-looking people-search sites safe? Many are advertising or data-selling businesses. Using the official source directly avoids that.
